To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) The level effect of the rate of population change is non-negative (and positive in the empirically relevant case), while the level effect of population size is a priori ambiguous.
the level effects of demographic variables are non-negative for the average level and ambiguous for the level, and the growth effects are positive for the average level but ambiguous for the level.
the long-run effects of population size and growth on per capita human and economic capital are negative, positive, or zero depending on the preference and technology parameters.
In summary, our research is concerned with

a more complete understanding of the mechanisms and the time dynamics of the impact of demographic changes on economic development, which is of great importance in view of the demographic transition in the developing countries.
the long-term effects of population change on economic development, which is of crucial importance in understanding the demographic transition process.
the mechanisms through which population growth affects the economy, and it shows that the level effects of the rate of population change are non-trivial.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the level effect is negative, the long-run growth effect is positive, and the short-run growth effect is negative.
population growth and size are detrimental to the economic performance of countries, in the short run as well as in the long run.
the growth effect of population change is always positive, while its level effect is ambiguous.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the growth and level effects of population change are not necessarily in the same direction.
the long-run effects of population change on the economy depend on a complex interaction of the different transmission mechanisms of the demographic shocks.
the long-run effect of population growth is ambiguous and depends on the preference and technology parameters.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the level effect is not negligible and that the long-term relationship between demography and the economy is more complicated than the existing theoretical literature suggests.
the long-run impact and the dynamic pattern of population changes depend on the interplay of the different mechanisms through which demography affects economic performance.
the level effects of demographic shocks are important and should not be neglected.
